rows.name: Number Passport: Figures, Words, Romans
steps: Each learner draws five number cards from a pile (numbers up to 10,000) to start a 'passport' page.
They write each number in figures and in words.
They round each number to the nearest 10 and the nearest 100 and mark the answer on a number line.
Give the chart of Roman numeral symbols; learners write three numbers under 100 in Roman numerals.
Learners find the rule in three given number sequences and write it as 'add 25 each time'.
Partners stamp or tick each other's passport page.
rows.materials: Number cards up to 10,000, passport sheets, Roman numeral chart, number line strips, sequence cards

levels.0: Writes figures but not words, or moves digits to the wrong place, and cannot say which 10 or 100 is nearer.
levels.1: Writes words for the numbers and rounds them using the number line and the Roman chart, with the spelling list on the board.
levels.2: Writes five numbers correctly in figures and words, rounds each to the nearest 10 and 100, and writes three Roman numerals and one sequence rule correctly.
levels.3: Builds the largest and smallest four-digit number from four digit cards, writes both in words and explains why 4,550 rounds up to 4,600.

rows.name: Market Stall Bar Models
steps: Run a 2-minute table quiz on cards up to 10 x 10 and note which facts were slow.
Show 36 x 4 as 30 x 4 plus 6 x 4 and also on a grid; learners do three more.
Share 48 pencils among 6 children by grouping, then by jumping back on a number line.
Give each group a two-step market story, such as '6 crates with 24 mangoes each, 40 are spoilt, the rest are packed 8 to a box'.
Groups draw a bar model and solve the problem.
Groups explain one bar model to another group.
rows.materials: Table cards, grid paper, number line strips, story cards, squared paper, pencils

levels.0: Draws no bar or draws one that does not match the story, and leaves the grid or number line incomplete.
levels.1: Completes 2-digit by 1-digit products using a partly filled grid and draws the bar model only after a template with two bars is given.
levels.2: Multiplies by partitioning, divides by jumping back correctly and solves the two-step story with a bar model that labels each part.
levels.3: Rewrites the mango story with new numbers, draws a new bar model and explains to another group why the second step needs division.

rows.name: Science Week Fizzy Experiment Station
steps: Choose a simple experiment such as the baking soda and vinegar balloon; show the equipment.
Groups write a question to test, such as 'Does more baking soda make the balloon bigger?'.
Groups predict the result and write it down.
Groups do the experiment, changing only the amount of baking soda each time.
Groups record the balloon size for each amount.
Groups explain to the class what happened and whether the prediction was right.
rows.materials: Baking soda, vinegar, small bottles, balloons, spoons, ruler or string, recording sheet

levels.0: Mixes ingredients without measuring and records no result on the sheet.
levels.1: Does the experiment with an educator-led checklist and writes the result using sentence starters.
levels.2: Changes only the amount of baking soda, records the balloon size for each trial, and states what happened.
levels.3: Suggests a second thing to change in a new test, such as the amount of vinegar, and explains how to keep it fair.

rows.name: Missing Number Mystery Cards
rows.unit: Addition and Subtraction of Whole Numbers
steps: Give each pair 10 cards, each showing an equation with one box hidden, such as 4,350 + __ = 6,000 or __ - 2,478 = 1,300.
Pairs solve each card and write the missing number on a slip.
Beside each answer they write M (mental) or W (written) and one sentence on why they chose that way.
Pairs add two odd numbers and two even numbers of their own choosing, three times each, and record the sums.
Pairs finish the sentence: 'An odd plus an odd always gives ___ because ___.'
Pairs swap cards and check each other's answers by reversing the operation.
rows.materials: Prepared equation cards, slips of paper, pencils, 4-digit number cards for the odd/even test

levels.0: Leaves the box blank on most cards or writes a number that makes the equation false when checked, and gives no strategy label.
levels.1: Finds the missing number on cards only when allowed to use a number line or counters, and the M/W choice is given by the partner.
levels.2: Fills the missing number correctly on at least eight of ten cards and tags each with M or W plus a short reason such as 'friendly numbers, so in my head'.
levels.3: Makes up a new missing-number card for a partner, and explains with a pair of examples why two even numbers can never make an odd sum.

rows.name: Certain, Likely, Unlikely, Impossible Bag Game
steps: Show four labels on the board: certain, likely, unlikely, impossible.
Read out ten events (the sun rises tomorrow, a coin lands on its edge, it rains in June) and have groups place each under a label.
Fill a bag with 5 red and 1 blue cube. Ask groups to predict which colour will be pulled out and why.
Groups list every possible outcome of tossing a coin, then of spinning a 4-colour spinner, on a recording sheet.
Groups draw from the bag 20 times, returning the cube each time, and tally the results.
Compare tallies with the predictions and discuss.
rows.materials: Cloth bag, coloured cubes, coin, paper spinner with pencil and paper clip, label cards, recording sheet

levels.0: Places most events under one label or leaves the outcome list empty, saying 'anything can happen'.
levels.1: Sorts the events correctly after the partner reads aloud the scale, and lists outcomes only with the spinner in hand to point at.
levels.2: Places events under the four labels sensibly and writes all outcomes for the coin (H, T) and the 4-colour spinner without missing one.
levels.3: Adds a new bag mix to make a given colour 'unlikely' and lists every outcome of tossing a coin and rolling a die together.

rows.name: Factor Rainbows and Split Products
steps: Give each learner a number from 12 to 48 on a card.
Using the tables, they list all factor pairs and draw a rainbow arc joining each pair.
Show how to mentally work 14 x 6 as 10 x 6 plus 4 x 6, and let learners try three of their own.
Learners work two further products, such as 34 x 7, by the written column method.
Partners check each other's column working against the split method for one product.
Share any pair where the two methods did not agree and find the slip.
rows.materials: Number cards, plain paper, coloured pencils, multiplication table chart for support

levels.0: Lists only 1 and the number itself as factors, and leaves the multiplications unworked or without any written steps.
levels.1: Finds factor pairs only while pointing along the table chart, and splits one number into parts when a worked example is left on the desk.
levels.2: Draws a complete rainbow of factor pairs for the number and gets the split mental product and the column product both correct.
levels.3: Spots a number with an odd count of factors, explains why with the rainbow, and picks the faster of the two methods for a new product, saying why.

rows.name: Shape Detectives and Tile Floors
steps: Hold up hidden shapes one at a time through a folder, describing only the number of sides and corners; groups name each shape.
Give each group paper cut-outs of a triangle, square, hexagon and regular pentagon and ask which will cover a sheet with no gaps.
Groups tile a sheet with their chosen shape by tracing it and glue it down as a tessellation.
On a second set of shapes, learners fold or use a mirror to draw all lines of symmetry in a different colour.
Learners draw the reflection of an L-shape across a mirror line drawn on grid paper.
Groups display their work and say which shapes would not tile.
rows.materials: Paper shape cut-outs, A3 sheets, glue, small mirrors, grid paper, coloured pencils

levels.0: Leaves gaps and overlaps in the tiling and draws no symmetry lines or a reflection that is not on the opposite side of the mirror line.
levels.1: Tiles the sheet with a square only, and draws symmetry lines or the reflection after checking with a mirror held by the educator.
levels.2: Covers the sheet with a repeated shape with no gaps, draws the correct lines of symmetry on two shapes and reflects the L-shape accurately on the grid.
levels.3: Predicts before trying that regular pentagons will leave gaps and explains it, and reflects a new shape across a diagonal mirror line.

rows.name: Fraction Strips and Sharing Snacks
steps: Give each learner three equal paper strips and have them fold into halves, quarters and eighths.
Learners shade equal parts of a drawn rectangle to show 3/4, 2/8 and 1/2.
Learners mark the same fractions on a number line from 0 to 1 drawn on a long strip.
Set out 12 counters as 'biscuits'; learners find a half and a quarter and write what they found.
Learners create a fraction card for a partner to shade and place on the line.
Partners check one another's cards.

levels.0: Shades unequal parts or marks fractions at random points between 0 and 1, and cannot say how many counters make a half.
levels.1: Shades fractions correctly when using the folded strip as a guide, and places marks on the line only when the partner has marked the halves.
levels.2: Shades equal parts for each fraction, places 3/4 and 1/2 correctly on the line and shares 12 counters into a half (6) and a quarter (3).
levels.3: Finds a quarter of a different amount such as 20 stickers and explains to a partner why 2/4 and 1/2 land on the same spot on the line.

rows.name: Robot Walk on the Floor Grid
steps: Mark a 6 x 6 grid on the floor with tape or chalk and place a few objects as landmarks.
One learner is the 'robot' and follows left, right, clockwise, anti-clockwise, quarter-turn and half-turn commands called by a partner.

Pairs choose a start and a finish square and write directions for the route in boxes on a sheet.
Another pair follows the written directions on the floor and records where the robot ends.
Discuss any route that went wrong and fix the directions.

levels.1: Follows turn words correctly when the partner points, and writes a route with sentence starters such as 'Go forward __ squares, then turn __'.
levels.2: Calls and follows quarter, half and full turns accurately and writes a route that another pair can walk to the exact finish square.
levels.3: Spots and fixes a deliberate error in a written route, and writes a shorter route to the same finish square.

levels.1: Finds the busiest day or dish with the educator pointing at the column, and decides with a sentence starter.
levels.2: Names a pattern in the table and uses it to choose how many of each dish to make, giving the reason.
levels.3: Changes the decision for a day with unusual data, such as a holiday, and explains why the pattern might not hold.

rows.name: Computer types gallery walk
steps: Stick six pictures around the room: desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, smart watch, a large server or supercomputer.
In pairs, walk round and write the name of each computer on a recording sheet.
Beside each name, write one thing it is used for.
Come back together and compare answers, fixing any wrong names.
Each pair picks their favourite and tells the class where they have seen it used.
rows.materials: Six printed pictures, recording sheet per pair, pencils

levels.0: Recording sheet has few names and no uses written, or the same use is repeated for every picture.
levels.1: Names the computers with the picture labels as a word bank, and gives a use only for the familiar ones like phone and laptop.
levels.2: Names at least one computer type correctly and writes a fitting use, such as laptop for homework or smart watch for checking time and steps.
levels.3: Points to a computer in real life, such as a ticket machine or a car display, names its type and explains what job it does there.

rows.name: Who does the job? Person, computer or robot
steps: Read out a list of tasks, such as solving a long sum, vacuuming a floor, comforting a sad friend, sorting parcels, drawing a funny cartoon.
Students move to one of three corners: 'Person only', 'Computer or robot can do it', 'Both'.
In each corner, students tell a neighbour why they chose it.
Pick one task and hear a reason from each corner.
Each student writes one task a computer or robot can do without a person helping each time.
Share a few and talk about tasks that still need a person.
rows.materials: List of tasks read aloud, three corner signs, paper slips

levels.0: Moves with the crowd to a corner and the slip is blank or names a task that needs a person each time.
levels.1: Names a task like vacuuming only after hearing the task list again or a partner's idea.
levels.2: During Who does the job? Person, computer or robot, writes or says one task a computer or robot does on its own, such as a washing machine running a cycle or a robot arm sorting parcels.
levels.3: Explains in their own example, such as an automatic door or a lift, what it does alone and which part still needs a person to set it up.

rows.name: News bulletin read-aloud
steps: Each day one student picks a short, suitable news item the educator has pre-checked.
The student practises reading it twice quietly, marking where to pause.
Standing at the front, the student reads it aloud like a news presenter, facing the class.
Listeners jot one fact they heard.
Two listeners share their fact and the reader confirms.
The educator gives one praise and one tip about pace or voice.
rows.materials: Printed or cut-out news item, highlighter, a 'news desk' table

levels.0: Does not read the item aloud, or reads so quietly that listeners cannot name a fact.
levels.1: Reads aloud with the educator or a partner reading along and the pause marks already made.
levels.2: Reads the whole item aloud clearly enough that listeners can state at least one fact.
levels.3: Reads fluently with pauses and tone, then answers a listener's question about the story in their own words.

rows.name: Assembly slot rehearsal
steps: Assign each student or small group a short assembly item such as a thought for the day, a one-minute talk or a poem.
Students write or choose their script on a card, three to five lines.
Rehearse in pairs: practise standing straight, a loud voice and eye contact.
Do a dress rehearsal on the actual stage or front of the hall with a few classmates as audience.
Audience gives one thing they heard clearly and one thing to improve.
Deliver at assembly and note it on a class sheet.
rows.materials: Script cards, microphone if available, a stage or hall area

levels.0: Does not speak at the rehearsal or stands silent after the first line.
levels.1: Speaks to the group with the script card read line by line and a partner prompting the next line.
levels.2: Speaks their lines to the audience in a voice the back row can hear.
levels.3: Speaks with eye contact and a steady voice, and answers a surprise question from the audience without the card.

rows.name: Five-minute tidy and pack check
steps: Give each student a pictured checklist: desk clear, bag packed, bottle in, homework diary in, chair pushed in.
Set a visible five-minute timer for the end of day.
Students tidy and pack on their own, ticking each item as they go.
Partners check each other's bag against the list.
The educator walks round and reminds anyone who missed an item; nothing is written down about any child.
Review in a circle: what slowed anyone down and how to fix it tomorrow.
rows.materials: Pictured checklist per student, timer, school bags and desks

rows.name: Word of the day sentence wall
steps: Write the word of the day on the board and read it aloud together.
Say what it means with a quick picture or action.
Students think of a sentence with the word and say it to a partner.
Each writes their own sentence on a sticky note.
Stick notes on the word wall under the word.
Read three or four aloud and check the word is used correctly.
rows.materials: Board, sticky notes, word wall space, pencils

levels.0: Sticky note is blank or copies the example sentence from the board.
levels.1: Writes a sentence with the word using the sentence starter on the board, such as 'The ___ was...'.
levels.2: Writes and says an original sentence in which the word fits its meaning.
levels.3: Uses the word correctly in a second, different context and explains how it differs from a similar word.

rows.name: Rapid-fire class quiz teams
steps: Split the class into four teams and give each a team name.
Educator prepares 12 questions from recent lessons across subjects.
Ask one question at a time; teams confer for 15 seconds.
A different team member answers each round.
Score on the board: one point per correct answer, with hints allowed for half a point.
Finish by listing questions that were missed and revisit them.
rows.materials: Question list, whiteboard for scores, team name cards

levels.0: Does not offer an answer when it is their turn, or answers unrelated to the question.
levels.1: Answers after the team discusses it, or after a hint such as the first letter or a picture.
levels.2: Answers their own question aloud when it is their turn, with a correct answer or a sensible attempt.
levels.3: Answers correctly and explains how they know, or builds on a teammate's wrong answer to correct it.

rows.name: Silent reading stamina log
steps: Each student picks a book from the class shelf or their own bag before reading time starts.
Set a timer for 15 minutes and everyone reads in quiet.
The educator circulates and notes who is still reading at the 5, 10 and 15 minute marks.
At the end, students write the page they reached in a reading log.
Partners tell each other in one sentence what happened in their pages.
Chart the class stamina weekly.
rows.materials: Class library books, reading logs, timer

levels.0: Stops reading within a couple of minutes and is looking around or doing something else, with the log left empty.
levels.1: Reads for most of the time when sitting beside the educator or a reading buddy, or after swapping to an easier book.
levels.2: Reads the same book for the whole period and logs the pages reached.
levels.3: Reads the whole time and tells a partner what happened and what they predict, using details from the pages.

rows.name: Mental maths ladder
steps: Draw a ladder with ten rungs on the board, easy at the bottom to harder at the top.
Read out a question for each rung, such as 7 x 8, 45 + 38, 100 - 63, half of 86.
Students write only the answer on a mini whiteboard and hold it up.
Check each round and record who is still climbing.
Ask two students to say the quick way they worked one answer out.
Everyone records their top rung in their notebook.
rows.materials: Mini whiteboards and markers, ladder drawing, question list

levels.0: Holds up a blank board or wrong answers even on the first few rungs.
levels.1: Gets the lower rungs right with a number line or table chart in view for support.
levels.2: Answers most of the questions correctly in their head, reaching the middle rungs or beyond.
levels.3: Reaches the top rungs and explains a fast strategy, such as doubling then adding one for 7 x 8 or rounding for 45 + 38.

rows.name: Evaluation task self-check routine
steps: Hand out the evaluation task and read the instructions aloud once.
Students underline the key words in each question.
They complete the task quietly in the set time.
Using a tick-box checklist, they check name, all questions answered and neat work.
They circle one question they found tricky.
Collect and note which circled questions repeat.
rows.materials: The evaluation task paper, pencils, tick-box checklist, timer

levels.0: Leaves several questions unanswered and the checklist unticked, with no sign of using the time.
levels.1: Completes the task after the educator reads out the instruction line by line or helps with the first question.
levels.2: Completes every question within the time and ticks the self-check list.
levels.3: Completes the task, spots and fixes one of their own mistakes with the checklist, and explains why the circled question was tricky.

rows.name: Paper and string No Screen Day challenge
steps: Announce the no-screen challenge: build a model or game from paper, string and cardboard.
In pairs, plan the idea by drawing a quick sketch.
Gather materials and build for about 25 minutes.
Test it: does it work, move or play?
Improve it once based on the test.
Show it to another pair and explain how it works.
rows.materials: Scrap paper, string, cardboard, tape, scissors, crayons

levels.0: Starts the sketch but leaves without a finished model, or asks to use a device instead.
levels.1: Finishes a simple model by copying the educator's example or following a partner's lead.
levels.2: Completes a working hands-on creation without a screen and shows it to another pair.
levels.3: Improves the design after testing and explains in their own words which change worked and why.

rows.name: Letter scramble race
steps: Prepare envelopes with scrambled letters of words from the current unit, for example 'tarsp' for 'parts'.
Pairs open an envelope and arrange the letters to find the word.
They write the word on a slip and check it in the word list.
Move on to the next envelope, with harder words later.
After ten minutes, pairs compare their words and read them aloud.
Pairs pick one word and use it in a sentence.
rows.materials: Envelopes with letter cards, word list, slips, pencils

levels.0: Moves the letters around but writes no complete word or an invented one that is not in the list.
levels.1: Unscrambles shorter words with the first letter given or a picture clue.
levels.2: Unscrambles several words correctly and writes each on the slip.
levels.3: Unscrambles the long words and then writes their own scrambled word for another pair to solve.

rows.note: built from the unit's syllabus bullets; no activity in the planning sheets; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Themed word search hunt
steps: Give each student a 10 by 10 grid containing eight words on a class theme, such as animals or food, with the word list beside it.
Tell students words can run across, down or diagonally.
Students find and circle each word, crossing it off the list.
Compare with a partner and help find any missing word.
Choose three words and write a sentence for each.
Students make a small 6 by 6 word search for a partner with four words.
rows.materials: Printed word search grid and word list, pencils, squared paper

levels.0: Circles letters that do not form any word on the list, or finds none.
levels.1: Finds the across words but needs a partner to point out the down and diagonal ones.
levels.2: Finds and circles all the listed words in the grid.
levels.3: Finds all words and builds a small word search of their own that a partner can solve.

rows.name: Riddle of the day
steps: Read a riddle aloud twice, slowly, such as 'I have hands but cannot clap. What am I?'.
Students think quietly, then whisper their answer to a partner.
Give one extra clue and let pairs try again.
Take answers and ask the pair to say which clue helped.
Reveal the answer and talk about the clue words.
Students write a riddle of their own and try it on another pair.
rows.materials: Riddle list, paper, pencils

levels.0: Gives no answer or guesses at random without using the clue words.
levels.1: Solves the riddle after the extra clue or a picture hint.
levels.2: Solves the riddle and names the clue word that led to the answer.
levels.3: Solves it and then writes a new riddle with two clear clues that a classmate can solve.

rows.name: Look, hide and draw from memory
steps: Place an everyday object, such as a water bottle or a leaf, where all can see it.
Students study it for one minute, noticing shape, parts and details.
Cover the object and students draw it from memory in five minutes.
Uncover it and students compare their drawings with the real object.
Add any missed details in a different colour.
Share one detail they remembered and one they missed.
rows.materials: Everyday object, cloth to cover it, paper, pencils, colour pencils

levels.0: Page stays blank or the drawing shows a shape unrelated to the object.
levels.1: Draws the main shape after a second look at the object or after a partner describes its parts.
levels.2: Draws the object from memory with its main shape and several parts in place.
levels.3: Draws the object with fine details such as texture and proportions, and names which details were added in the second colour.

rows.name: Classroom spelling bee rounds
steps: Prepare a list of 20 words from the week, ordered easy to hard.
Students sit in a circle; the educator says a word, uses it in a sentence and says it again.
The student whose turn it is spells the word aloud.
If correct, they stay in; if incorrect, the next student may try.
Write missed words on the board and spell them together.
Students copy missed words three times for next time.
rows.materials: Word list, whiteboard, notebooks

levels.0: Says letters that do not match the word or cannot attempt it when called on.
levels.1: Spells the word aloud after hearing it in a sentence and a repeat, with a syllable clap.
levels.2: Spells their word correctly aloud, letter by letter.
levels.3: Spells a harder word correctly and names the spelling rule or trick that helped, such as 'i before e'.

rows.note: built from the unit's syllabus bullets; no activity in the planning sheets; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Theme web across two subjects
steps: Announce the theme, for example 'Water'.
On chart paper, draw a web with the theme in the middle and two branches for two subjects, such as science and geography.
Groups list three ideas under each branch.
Draw lines between ideas that connect across the two subjects.
Groups make a one-page poster showing the links.
Present the poster, naming at least one link.
rows.materials: Chart paper, markers, textbooks for reference

levels.0: The web has ideas from only one subject and no lines linking them.
levels.1: Adds a link between subjects after the educator gives a sentence starter such as 'This is like... because...'.
levels.2: Draws and explains at least one link between an idea from each subject on the poster.
levels.3: Shows two or more links and uses one to answer a new question from the class, such as how the theme affects people in a nearby place.

rows.note: built from the unit's syllabus bullets; no activity in the planning sheets; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Rules-first relay team game
steps: Explain a simple team game, such as a relay or throwball, and write its three main rules on a board.
Teams repeat the rules back in their own words.
Play a first round and the educator watches for rule breaks.
Pause and discuss one rule break that happened and why the rule exists.
Play a second round with a team captain keeping the rules.
Cool down and teams say one thing they did well as a team.
rows.materials: Cones or markers, a ball or batons, rules board

levels.0: Joins in but ignores the rules, such as running early or leaving the lane, and does not respond to reminders.
levels.1: Follows the rules in the game when the captain or educator reminds them before each turn.
levels.2: Plays the whole game with the team and follows its rules without reminders.
levels.3: Plays by the rules, encourages teammates, and explains a rule or suggests a fairer rule after the game.

rows.name: Outfit choice show and tell
steps: Ask students to wear an outfit of their choice and think about why they chose it.
In a circle, each student stands and shows their outfit.
Complete the sentence 'I chose this because...'.
Listeners say one thing they noticed about the outfit.
Group the reasons on the board: comfort, colour, weather, occasion, favourite.
Say one reason you would choose the same outfit again.
rows.materials: Students' own clothes, board, markers

Stays still and looks at the speaker while others show their outfits
Names one thing noticed about a classmate's outfit

rows.name: Mini mock Olympiad paper
steps: Prepare a short mock paper of 10 questions mixing maths and reasoning, with multiple-choice answers.
Explain how to fill the answer sheet and the time limit.
Students attempt the paper in 25 minutes in quiet.
Collect and mark with the class using an answer key.
Students tick the questions they attempted, got right or skipped.
Discuss two questions many found tricky and how to approach them.
rows.materials: Printed mock paper and answer sheet, key, pencils, timer

levels.0: Attempts very few questions and the answer sheet is mostly blank.
levels.1: Attempts most questions with the instructions read aloud and a worked example on the board.
levels.2: Attempts the paper in the time limit, filling the answer sheet in the correct format.
levels.3: Attempts the whole paper, chooses which questions to leave for later, and explains how they approached one of the tricky questions.

rows.name: Magazine story read and retell
steps: Set out copies of the magazine or printed story pages.
Students pick one story and read it silently.
They list the characters and the problem on a card.
In pairs, they retell the story in their own words.
The listener asks one question about the story.
Students rate the story with a star sign and say why.
rows.materials: Magazine copies or printed stories, cards, pencils

levels.0: During Magazine story read and retell, looks at the magazine pages but cannot say anything about what the story was about.
levels.1: Reads the story with a partner or the educator and names the characters using the card prompts.
levels.2: Reads the story through and retells it to a partner with the main characters and the problem.
levels.3: Reads and retells the story, then predicts what might happen next and gives a reason from the story.

rows.name: Block city build challenge
steps: Divide the class into small groups with a set of building blocks.
Set a challenge: build the tallest tower that can stand, or a bridge between two desks.
Groups sketch a quick plan, then build for 15 minutes.
Test the build: does it stand or hold a small weight?
Groups fix one problem and test again.
Groups explain their building to another group.
rows.materials: Building blocks, scrap paper for plans, small weights such as a pencil case

levels.0: Handles the blocks but does not put them together into a structure.
levels.1: Builds a simple stack or wall with a partner showing how to balance the blocks.
levels.2: Builds a structure from the blocks that stands up on its own.
levels.3: Builds a structure that meets the challenge, then rebuilds it stronger and explains what made it more stable.

rows.name: Class crossword solve
steps: Give each pair a small crossword with five across and five down clues from a current unit.
Read the clues together and solve the ones they are sure of first.
Use crossing letters to help with harder clues.
Check spelling against the word list at the end.
Pairs choose one answer and say it in a sentence.
Pairs write one new clue for a word of their own.
rows.materials: Printed crossword, word list, pencils, erasers

levels.0: Fills in only one or two boxes, or letters do not fit the clue or the crossing words.
levels.1: Fills in most of the grid with the word list beside them and a partner's help with the crossing words.
levels.2: Completes the crossword with correct answers that fit the clues and crossing letters.
levels.3: Completes the crossword and writes a good clue for a new word that a classmate can solve.

rows.name: My favourite place short essay
steps: Give the topic 'My favourite place' and ask students to jot three things about it.
Plan with a simple frame: opening sentence, two details, a closing thought.
Write the essay in about 10 minutes, 8 to 10 sentences.
Reread silently, checking capital letters and full stops.
Swap with a partner who underlines their favourite sentence.
Share a few aloud.
rows.materials: Notebooks, pencils, planning frame on the board

levels.0: Writes only a title or a sentence or two that does not stay on the topic.
levels.1: Writes the essay using the planning frame and sentence starters on the board.
levels.2: Writes a short essay on the topic with an opening, details and a closing sentence.
levels.3: Writes an essay that includes vivid detail or a comparison, and revises one sentence after the partner's comment.

rows.name: Doodle, then describe it
steps: Students make a doodle of any kind in two minutes from a starting squiggle.
Give a prompt: What does it look like? What is it doing?
Students write 3 to 5 sentences describing the doodle.
Underline two describing words.
Swap with a partner who tries to draw the doodle from the description only.
Compare the drawing to the original.

levels.0: Draws the doodle but writes nothing or only labels it with one word.
levels.1: Writes sentences about the doodle using the prompt questions and a describing-word list.
levels.2: Writes several sentences that describe what the doodle shows, with at least two describing words.
levels.3: Writes a description detailed enough that a partner draws a similar picture from the words alone.

rows.name: Four by four sudoku solve
steps: Show a 4 by 4 sudoku on the board and explain the rule: each row, column and box has 1 to 4 once.
Solve one square together, explaining each step.
Pairs get their own 4 by 4 puzzle with half the cells filled in.
Fill in the cells they can be sure of, in pencil.
Check each row, column and box.
Faster pairs try a 6 by 6 puzzle.

levels.0: Writes numbers that repeat in a row or box, and the grid is far from complete.

levels.2: Completes the 4 by 4 sudoku with every row, column and box correct.
levels.3: Completes a larger puzzle and explains why a certain cell had to be a particular number.

rows.name: Two-voice dialogue script
steps: Pair students and give a scene such as two friends deciding what game to play at break.
Each takes one character and talks the scene aloud first.
Write the dialogue on paper, using a new line and speech marks for each speaker.
Include at least six turns, with a name or dash before each speaker's words.
Read it aloud together with expression.
Another pair listens and says if it sounds natural.

levels.0: Writes lines of talk with no sign of who is speaking, or only a single line.

levels.2: Writes at least six turns of dialogue between two people, each on a new line with the speaker clear.
levels.3: Writes a dialogue with natural, distinct voices and adds speech marks or action words, and reads it aloud with expression.

Lead slow breathing together for a minute.

Close with a calm minute of quiet breathing.
